So it's worth understanding that the Institute has a clear advocacy mission that doesn't automatically make its research invalid. In fact, some of its work uses legitimate scientific methods developed in collaboration with university researchers. But its own reports are not necessarily independently peer-reviewed scientific studies. Anyways, I found one of its research reports called The Real Truth, Women Aren't Seen or Heard that was published in 2016. The researchers analyzed 200 top-grossing non-animated films from 2014 and 2015. They found, among other things, that male characters received approximately twice as much screen time as female characters and spoke approximately twice as often in a film from 2015. What they didn't establish was the gender perception bias this lady is talking about. So I dug deeper and I found that the actress, Gina Davis herself, repeated the 17 and 33% claim in an NPR interview back in 2013. Anyways, one of the users claimed that Dale Spender had recorded mixed-gender university classroom discussions and found that men perceived conversations as equal when women spoke only 15% of the time. And when women spoke 30% of the time, men supposedly perceived them as dominating the conversation. The user attributed these findings to Spender's 1980 book, Men Made Language, but didn't provide a specific scientific study explaining how those numbers were obtained. That claim was then reproduced by some feminist website and the discussion later appeared on a blog called All Things Linguistic. And here's where things get interesting. In that discussion, two women, one identifying herself as a behavioral scientist and the other as a linguist, actually questioned Spender's research. The behavioral scientist raised concerns about Spender's research methodology, including the lack of information about the classrooms being studied. Although she acknowledged that she hadn't been able to fully access Spender's original work, she noted that Spender's work does not necessarily meet the academic standards And the linguist went even further, criticizing Spender's methodology and arguing that her theoretical conclusions suffered from confirmation bias. She also pointed out that subsequent studies had produced more complicated and sometimes conflicting findings. And remember, these criticisms came from women who were generally sympathetic to the original argument. Now, I also tried to verify the exact numerical findings in Spender's original work and other sources, but from the material I could access, I wasn't able to verify how those numbers were established. So where does all of this leave us? Despite looking through the sources attributed to Gina Davis and Dale Spender, I couldn't find scientific evidence establishing the specific numbers. Now, does that mean that the gender perception bias does not exist? No, it doesn't. What it means is that I couldn't verify the evidence and the numbers this lady provided in her video. So until she provides the research establishing these specific numbers, I don't think we should be treating the presented gender perception bias as some established data point. As of now, it seems to be just a talking point.
